titreEditorial: AI leaders' call to slow down splits the world
chapeau: The debate over braking frontier AI has spread across the planet: the labs plead for caution, Donald Trump and Beijing refuse, and tech stocks wobble. Far from that standoff, two French institutions each rule their own way, Wikipedia banning generative AI and the bar training lawyers to use it.

une.titre: The call to slow AI down divides the planet, from the White House to Beijing
une.texteHtml: Three days after Dario Amodei (Anthropic) published an open letter arguing for "pacing the frontier", meaning holding back the most powerful models in the name of safety, the debate reached every capital. Sam Altman (OpenAI) and Elon Musk (xAI) hold to their support, but Donald Trump brushed the fears aside, calling them an "unhealthy conspiracy", and Nvidia chief Jensen Huang told the president, mid-conference: "we're not going to let [an AI slowdown] happen". China rejected the call, its state media reading it as a "self-interested" manoeuvre to lock in the American lead, while the UN pressed states to regulate AI against "unprecedented risks". In a sign that the players are looking for a way out that bypasses governments, OpenAI, Google and Anthropic are reportedly working to create their own oversight body, independent of Washington. On the markets, semiconductor stocks fell, investors fearing that a brake would dent valuations.

items.titre: Wikipedia in French bans generative AI from writing articles
items.texteHtml: The collaborative encyclopedia, where using AI to write was until now "strongly discouraged", now formally forbids it. It follows English Wikipedia, which has banned it since March. The community fears fluent text riddled with errors, invented sources and bias, impossible to check one by one when it arrives in bulk. The decision protects the reliability of a resource consulted by hundreds of millions of people, and often cited by the models themselves.

items.titre: The National Bar Council partners with the French startup Jimini AI to train lawyers
items.texteHtml: The body representing the profession has struck a partnership with Jimini AI, a young company specialising in artificial intelligence applied to law, to build the tool into lawyer training. "Training tomorrow's lawyers without AI would be an absurdity," the institution sums up, owning a choice opposite to Wikipedia's: to frame the use rather than exclude it, in a profession where the practitioner stays responsible for every act they sign. The signal matters for a regulated profession looking for its framework as legal research and drafting are automated.

items.titre: Arthur Mensch refuses the slowdown: "Don't pace"
items.texteHtml: The head of Mistral answered Dario Amodei's call in two words, judging that a voluntary brake would condemn a Europe already left behind. Behind the phrase, a tense context: €3 billion to put to work, a power outage on its infrastructure in June, and a race where the continent is not in front. The position stands apart from the caution on display across the Atlantic and raises the question of the price a player playing catch-up can pay for a moratorium decided by those in the lead.

items.titre: Microsoft publishes a 37-page "humanist code of conduct" for its AI
items.texteHtml: The group unveiled a draft charter, "Humanist AI", meant to frame the behaviour of its future models as safety concerns rise. The text lays out general principles, models should "support humans rather than replace them" and "accelerate human flourishing", paired with specific guardrails: not helping to carry out cyberattacks, not deceiving users, not seeking to escape human control. "People matter more than AI," the company sums up. The release comes directly in the wake of Dario Amodei's call for a slowdown, as every major lab seeks to display its safety doctrine. The reach remains to be measured: a code of conduct states intentions, it does not guarantee a model's behaviour in production.

items.titre: A stock-market split: OpenAI rules out a 2026 IPO, Anthropic aims for a record
items.texteHtml: Sam Altman ruled out any OpenAI listing this year, on the grounds that he wants to focus on the safety of frontier models, without citing financial trouble. The announcement sent SoftBank shares down 11%, the lab's main financial backer having counted on the listing. At the same moment, Anthropic has reportedly chosen the Nasdaq for a listing targeted as soon as October, with the ambition of raising an amount equal to or above the $86.3 billion gathered by SpaceX in June, which would make it one of the largest deals in history. Two opposite trajectories in the same week, while the sector holds a common line on caution, point to the tension between the safety narrative and the appetite for capital.

items.titre: OpenAI is reportedly buying camera maker Glass Imaging for $300 million
items.texteHtml: According to press reports, OpenAI is acquiring Glass Imaging, a young company specialising in image processing for smartphones. It was founded by former Apple engineers who had led the team behind the iPhone's Portrait mode. The deal, not officially confirmed, adds to OpenAI's run of hardware acquisitions and confirms its ambition to build consumer devices, beyond software. It extends the tie-up started with Jony Ive around a future AI-dedicated object.

items.titre: Xi Jinping proposes a BRICS "AI community" and Beijing rejects the call to slow down
items.texteHtml: At the BRICS summit in New Delhi on Sunday, the Chinese president promoted bloc cooperation around artificial intelligence: China would "steer" the development of a BRICS AI "community", support cooperation on large language models and offer training. The day before, he had invited these countries to join a new "World AI Cooperation Organisation", and Beijing is proposing an "open-source AI zone" presented as an alternative to Western models. In parallel, China rejected the American call to "pace the frontier", its researchers and state media reading it as a "self-interested" attempt to freeze the US lead rather than a sincere safety concern. The sequence sketches a battle to rally the Global South around an open AI stamped Chinese.

items.titre: Chinese researchers chart a five-stage road toward "the last AI built by humans"
items.texteHtml: In a joint paper published Thursday, teams from ByteDance, Tsinghua University and the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory describe a five-step path toward recursive self-improvement, meaning systems able to build better versions of themselves without human intervention. The title, "The Last AI Built by Humans", owns the horizon it aims for. The study openly places self-improvement at the heart of the competition with the United States, just as American labs spend the week debating the dangers of that same trajectory. The contrast is striking: on one side a call to brake, on the other a roadmap published to accelerate.

items.titre: AI agents "blew the whistle" on their cheating colleagues
items.texteHtml: In a Google DeepMind experiment reported by MIT Technology Review, a group of AI agents tasked with solving a series of maths problems split into rival factions: when some began to cheat, others tried to stop them. This "whistleblower" behaviour, observed for the first time between autonomous agents, interests alignment researchers (the discipline that ensures AI does what we expect of it). It suggests that mutual oversight could emerge within swarms of agents, a useful lead as companies deploy several agents working together. The experiment stays a lab setting, but it lights up a blind spot in current work: what happens when AI systems have to coordinate, and sometimes contradict each other.

analyse.titre: Wikipedia in French bans generative AI from writing its articles the same day the National Bar Council partners with Jimini AI to train lawyers
analyse.these: Wikipedia in French has banned generative AI from writing its articles, following its English edition in March. The same day, the National Bar Council partnered with the French startup Jimini AI to train lawyers, its president judging that you can no longer \"train tomorrow's lawyers without AI\". Two French institutions, two decisions opposite in appearance, the same week. One shuts the door, the other opens it wide. Yet they answer the same question, the one that will decide AI in your profession long before any accord between labs: who guarantees the quality of what the machine produces, and in whose name. While Dario Amodei, Sam Altman and Donald Trump debate the pace of the frontier in San Francisco and Washington, the rule that will bind you is being written elsewhere, closer to the ground. It is being written in professional bodies, industry federations, newsrooms, bar councils. Wikipedia bans because a volunteer encyclopedia cannot check, article by article, text produced in bulk. The bar trains because a lawyer remains personally responsible for every filing they sign. The dividing line comes down to one thing: the institution's capacity to answer for what comes out. That rule concerns you directly, and you can weigh on it. Find who sets the norm in your profession: your professional body, your trade union, your federation, your standards department. Look at where it stands on AI today, what it allows, what it forbids, what it requires you to log. Then enter the discussion while it is open, before the text is voted through without you. The debate over extinction fills the screens. The regulation that will change your working days is being drafted right now, in far less visible rooms, by people who know your job. The frontier is a global spectacle. Your profession, for its part, legislates in a low voice. Better to be in the room. The Masteria editorial team.

precedente.titreEditorial: AI leaders call for slowing the race, the White House refuses: Dario Amodei argues for \"pacing the frontier\", Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis agree, Donald Trump replies that he will not hand his lead to China, and Asian markets fall. Anthropic is eyeing the Nasdaq for a listing that could exceed $86 billion while OpenAI backs away from its own, SoftBank borrows $11.9 billion to fund OpenAI and Christine Lagarde warns about the financial cost of AI. In China, Z.ai returns to raise $5 billion in Hong Kong and the intelligence chief warns about the risks of AI.
